meta.description: Yes — Simone Weil really wrote it, in a 13 April 1942 letter to poet Joë Bousquet. Here's the French original and where it's often mis-sourced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Simone Weil — from her 1942 letter to Joë Bousquet, not from Gravity and Grace as it's often cited. The documented source, verified.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Weil wrote this to the poet Joë Bousquet in a letter dated 13 April 1942; the French original reads “L’attention est la forme la plus rare et la plus pure de la générosité.” The familiar English wording comes from Raymond Rosenthal’s translation, and both the French line and its source are documented in Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗.

source.excerpt: Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.
trail: The line is genuine. Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ gives the French original and traces it to Weil’s 13 April 1942 letter to Joë Bousquet, published in their Correspondance (L’Age d’Homme, 1982), p. 18.
A scholar who tracked down the letter confirms the same French text and publication history — first printed in a 1950 issue of Cahiers du Sud — on Kathleen Fitzpatrick’s blog ↗.
The familiar English wording is attributed to Raymond Rosenthal’s translation (via Simone Pétrement’s biography) at the WIST quotations archive ↗.
The idea recurs across Weil’s work: a related medical-humanities study, ‘The Rarest and Purest Form of Generosity’ ↗, builds on the same theme.
source.excerptNote: Original French: “L’attention est la forme la plus rare et la plus pure de la générosité.” Weil wrote it to Joë Bousquet, a poet then bedridden with a grievous First World War injury, in response to the close attention he had given pages she had shared with him.

source.rightsNote: This is not a public-domain line. Weil wrote it in French in 1942 and it was first published in 1950; the widely quoted English wording comes from Raymond Rosenthal’s 1976 translation. Under U.S. rules a work first published in 1931 or later remains in copyright, so both the French letter (as collected) and the English rendering are protected — the rights resting with Weil’s estate and, for the translation, the translator and publisher.

author.name: Simone Weil
author.heading: About Simone Weil
author.bio: Simone Weil was a French philosopher, mystic, and political activist whose spare, intense writing on attention, affliction, and grace was mostly published after her early death in 1943. Attention — a disciplined, self-emptying openness to another person or to truth — sits at the centre of her thought, which is why the idea that attention is a form of generosity is so characteristically hers. Much of her work survives as notebooks, essays, and letters gathered posthumously into volumes such as Gravity and Grace and Waiting for God.

misattribution.heading: The catch: it's genuine, but often mis-sourced
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a “magnet” name, this one really is Simone Weil. The trouble is where people say it comes from — and that it almost always travels with no source at all.

items.who: Gravity and Grace / First and Last Notebooks
items.why: The line is frequently pinned to Weil’s notebook collections. It actually comes from her 1942 letter to Joë Bousquet; even a careful essay like The Marginalian ↗ files it under First and Last Notebooks.
On most quote aggregators the sentence appears with only “— Simone Weil” and no letter, date, or book, which is how genuine lines drift into looking apocryphal.

misattribution.truthLine: The real source is a letter Weil wrote to the poet Joë Bousquet on 13 April 1942, as documented in Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: For Weil, attention was not idle focus but a rare, self-emptying openness — “the rarest and purest form of generosity” precisely because giving someone your full attention means setting your own self aside to receive them. She was writing to Joë Bousquet, a poet left bedridden by a war wound, and thanking him for the very kind of careful attention she was describing.
That is why the line has outlived its private occasion: in an age of distraction it reframes simply noticing another person as an act of moral generosity.
context.pull: To give someone your undivided attention is, for Weil, to give them something of yourself.
